contextTopics.label: Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine
background: Russland überfiel die Ukraine am 24. Februar 2022 in vollem Umfang. Vorausgegangen war die Annexion der Krim im März 2014 und der von Russland unterstützte bewaffnete Konflikt im Donbas ab April 2014.

Die UN-Generalversammlung verurteilte den Angriff am 2. März 2022 mit 141 zu 5 Stimmen und forderte den sofortigen Rückzug. Die EU, die USA und weitere Staaten verhängten seither mehrere Sanktionspakete.
Der Internationale Strafgerichtshof erließ im März 2023 einen Haftbefehl gegen Wladimir Putin wegen der Verschleppung ukrainischer Kinder.
Österreich ist militärisch neutral, beteiligt sich aber an den EU-Sanktionen und leistet humanitäre Hilfe. Waffenlieferungen erfolgen nicht.

contextTopics.label: Krieg in Gaza und im Nahen Osten
background: Die Hamas verübte am 7. Oktober 2023 einen Großangriff auf Israel mit rund 1.200 Toten und etwa 250 Verschleppten. Israel begann daraufhin eine großangelegte Militäroperation im Gazastreifen.
Der Konflikt reicht weit zurück: Israel wurde 1948 gegründet, es folgten mehrere Kriege mit arabischen Nachbarstaaten. Der Gazastreifen wird seit 2007 von der Hamas kontrolliert.
Der Internationale Gerichtshof befasst sich seit Dezember 2023 mit einer Klage Südafrikas wegen mutmaßlichen Völkermords; ein Urteil in der Hauptsache steht aus.

Zahlenangaben zu Opfern stammen je nach Meldung von unterschiedlichen Stellen — der von der Hamas geführten Gesundheitsbehörde, israelischen Angaben oder UN-Organisationen. Sie sind selten unabhängig überprüfbar.

contextTopics.label: Handelskonflikte und Zölle
background: Die USA erhoben ab 2018 unter Präsident Trump Zölle auf Stahl, Aluminium und zahlreiche chinesische Waren. China antwortete mit Gegenzöllen. Teile davon blieben auch unter der Nachfolgeregierung bestehen.
Die EU ist als Zollunion für die Handelspolitik ihrer Mitgliedsstaaten zuständig — Österreich verhandelt also nicht selbst, sondern die Europäische Kommission.
Zölle wirken auf zwei Wegen: Sie verteuern eingeführte Waren für Verbraucher im Einfuhrland und treffen Exporteure im Ausland. Wer die Kosten trägt, ist wirtschaftswissenschaftlich umstritten.

contextTopics.label: Inflation und Zinspolitik der EZB
background: Die Europäische Zentralbank hat als vorrangiges Ziel Preisstabilität, definiert als 2 Prozent Inflation mittelfristig. Sie steuert darüber den Leitzins für den gesamten Euroraum.
Nach Jahren mit Null- und Negativzinsen begann die EZB im Juli 2022 mit Zinserhöhungen, um die stark gestiegene Inflation zu dämpfen — ausgelöst unter anderem durch Energiepreise und Lieferengpässe.

Österreich lag bei der Inflationsrate über Jahre über dem Euroraum-Durchschnitt. Die Gründe dafür sind umstritten; genannt werden unter anderem Energiepreise, Mietanpassungen und der Gastronomiesektor.

contextTopics.label: Klimapolitik und Klimaziele
background: Im Pariser Abkommen von 2015 verpflichteten sich fast alle Staaten, die Erderwärmung deutlich unter 2 Grad gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu halten und 1,5 Grad anzustreben.
Die EU hat sich auf Klimaneutralität bis 2050 festgelegt und Zwischenziele für 2030 beschlossen. Österreich strebt Klimaneutralität bis 2040 an — früher als die EU-Vorgabe.

Der Weltklimarat IPCC fasst regelmäßig den Forschungsstand zusammen. Dass die Erwärmung überwiegend menschengemacht ist, gilt dort als gesichert; umstritten sind Tempo, regionale Folgen und Gegenmaßnahmen.

contextTopics.label: Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz
background: Die Europäische Kommission legte 2021 den Entwurf für den AI Act vor, die weltweit erste umfassende Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz. Er stuft Anwendungen nach Risiko ein und verbietet einige ganz.
Das Gesetz gilt für Anbieter, die ihre Systeme im EU-Markt anbieten — unabhängig davon, wo sie sitzen. Die Pflichten greifen gestaffelt über mehrere Jahre.
Kritik kommt von zwei Seiten: Teilen der Industrie, die Wettbewerbsnachteile befürchten, und Bürgerrechtsorganisationen, denen die Ausnahmen für Sicherheitsbehörden zu weit gehen.

contextTopics.label: Österreichische Innenpolitik
background: Österreich ist eine parlamentarische Demokratie. Der Nationalrat mit 183 Abgeordneten wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt; die Regierung braucht dessen Vertrauen.
Der Bundespräsident wird direkt gewählt, ernennt die Regierung und kann sie entlassen — eine Befugnis, die historisch selten genutzt wurde.
Untersuchungsausschüsse sind ein Minderheitsrecht: Ein Viertel der Abgeordneten kann einen einsetzen, ohne Zustimmung der Mehrheit.

contextTopics.label: Raiffeisen Bank International
background: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist eine der größten Banken Österreichs mit Schwerpunkt in Zentral- und Osteuropa. Sie ging 2010 aus der Fusion von RZB-Teilen und Raiffeisen International hervor.
Der Raiffeisen-Sektor ist genossenschaftlich aufgebaut: lokale Raiffeisenbanken, darüber Landesbanken, darüber die RBI. Diese Struktur erklärt, warum Entscheidungen oft mehrere Ebenen betreffen.
Das Russland-Geschäft der RBI steht seit dem Angriff auf die Ukraine unter besonderer Beobachtung von EZB und US-Behörden. Ein Rückzug wurde mehrfach angekündigt und verzögerte sich.

items.title: 🇨🇵 L’IA nous rend du temps : faisons enfin du vrai Product Management
items.summary: Des LLMs impressionnants… et pas (encore) créatifs Soyons clairs : je suis loin d’être un détracteur de l’IA générative. Les LLMs écrivent du code, des tests, de la documentation, des synthèses, et ils le font à une vitesse qui était inimaginable il y a peu. Je les utilise, et vous aussi probablement. Mais plus je les pratique, plus un constat s’impose : ils excellent à produire du plausible. Ils recombinent, reformulent, complètent ce qui existe déjà. Ce qu’ils savent beaucoup moins faire, du moins aujourd’hui, c’est ce que nous faisons naturellement : remarquer ce que personne n’a demandé, relier deux idées qui n’ont rien à voir, ressentir un malaise face à un produit qui « fonctionne » mais qui n’a pas de sens. Ou encore prendre le risque d’un pari. Cette créativité, cette capacité à bâtir une vision à partir d’évidences, l’IA générative actuelle ne l’a pas. Et c’est précisément ce qui devrait nous préoccuper dans la manière dont nous allons utiliser le temps qu’elle nous fait gagner. Le réflexe : toujours plus 🏭 Dans beaucoup de comités de direction, le raisonnement est déjà posé : si l’IA rend les développeurs 30 % plus rapides, il en faut moins. Même production, équipe plus petite, coûts réduits. C’est logique, mais cela suppose que le problème de nos produits était la quantité (output) de fonctionnalités livrées. Nous avons presque tous croisé une feature factory : une roadmap de promesses, un succès mesuré à ce qui part en production plutôt qu’à ce qui change pour l’utilisateur (Melissa Perri parle de build trap). Or, quand construire coûte moins cher, le réflexe naturel est de demander plus. L’IA ne sort pas la feature factory de son piège, elle lui donne un turbo. Et notre excuse préférée, « on n’a pas le temps pour la Discovery », a disparu ! Mais aller plus vite ne mènera pas bien loin 🚤 Même si cette course au volume fonctionnait, elle se heurterait à deux limites. La première : tout le monde accélère. Vos concurrents ont les mêmes outils, les mêmes assistants, la même capacité à générer du code en quelques minutes. La vitesse devient un ticket d’entrée, plus un avantage. Ce qui reste difficile à copier, c’est de savoir quoi construire et pourquoi, et cela nous ramène exactement à ce que les LLMs ne font pas : passer de douze conversations clients à une direction. La seconde : vos clients ne suivent pas forcément. Imaginons une mise en production quotidienne. Beaucoup de produits vivent dans le monde de quelqu’un d’autre, un autre contexte : utilisateurs à former, validations, environnements réglementés, intégrations, équipes support à préparer. Un client qui doit réapprendre ses outils chaque matin ne vit pas la vitesse comme de la valeur, mais comme du bruit. Le rythme utile est fixé par celui qui reçoit, pas par celui qui produit. Alors, ce temps gagné ? 🎯 Si produire plus ne nous distingue pas et que nos clients ne peuvent pas l’absorber, il reste une seule voie : réinvestir le temps libéré là où l’IA est la plus faible, c’est-à-dire dans notre créativité et notre compréhension de l’utilisateur. ▪️ Parler aux clients très régulièrement, pas une fois par trimestre ▪️ Explorer le problème avant de choisir une solution ▪️ Prototyper plusieurs pistes et les confronter à de vraies personnes proche de l'usage, pas vos collègues de bureau. ▪️ Observer, mesurer, analyser, comprendre l’usage réel dès la mise en production L’IA peut accélérer chacune de ces étapes (prototyper une idée en une après-midi rend l’expérimentation bon marché), mais elle ne les remplace pas. Un utilisateur synthétique (persona) n’est pas un client, et un résumé de notes, insights ou feedbacks clients ne vaut pas le fait d’entendre quelqu’un galérer avec votre produit. Et cela concerne toute l’équipe. Dans Scrum, le terme Developers est volontairement large : il couvre toute personne qui contribue à créer le produit avec une expertise et un regard utiles à son évolution (design, recherche, data, qualité, métier, ingénierie…). C’est d’autant plus vrai aujourd’hui. Si une partie du code se génère, ce qui compte devient ce que ces regards apportent : questionner le besoin, challenger une idée, imaginer une expérience. Réduire les équipes au nom de l’efficience, c’est risquer de se priver précisément de celles et ceux qui savent transformer le temps libéré en apprentissage. Pour résumer L’IA va rendre du temps à la plupart des équipes. Ce temps ira quelque part : vers plus de fonctionnalités, ou vers plus de compréhension, de créativité, de vision. Alors posez-vous cette question avec votre équipe : « Si nous avions demain deux fois plus de capacité de livraison, qu’en ferions-nous ? » Si la réponse honnête est « plus de la même chose », alors le problème n’a jamais été la vitesse 🏁 Vous avez aimé cet article ? items.title: A Team of AI Agents Needs Scrum, Not a Better Model
items.summary: "Agent = Model + Harness" describes one AI agent well and a team of agents badly. Once agents work together, the defects that matter come from handoffs, shared records and two agents doing the same work. A better model fixes none of those. A team needs a second line: Team = Agents + Coordination. Scrum already supplies the coordination. My own team of AI agents runs on Scrum, and its records show where the defects come from. The formula is right for one agent Vivek Trivedy of LangChain states the formula in exactly those words. He defines the harness as every piece of code, configuration and execution logic that isn't the model (Trivedy, 2026). The model supplies the reasoning and the writing. The harness is the software the agent runs in: it runs the loop, hands the agent its tools and decides what the agent sees. A better model makes one agent write better, and a better harness gets more done from the same model. A team of agents fails at the handoffs Put several agents on one piece of work and someone has to decide which agent takes which task. Every agent also needs the same current copy of the draft. Those are decisions about how the agents work together, so they sit outside any one agent's model. Any Scrum Master has seen the human version: capable Developers who still lose work in the handoff between them. I split coordination into four parts. The Scrum Guide covers each one (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020): Orchestration is who starts the work and in what order. In Scrum, the Product Owner orders the Product Backlog, the Developers plan the Sprint, and the Scrum Master makes sure the events take place, stay productive and keep to their timebox. Shared state is the record every agent reads and writes. In Scrum, that is the artifacts, such as the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog. Protocols are the rules for claiming work and handing it on. Scrum leaves these to the Scrum Team, which is self-managing: it decides who does what, when and how. Governance is what "done" means and who checks it. In Scrum, that is the Definition of Done. The Developers must meet it, and the Scrum Team inspects it at the Sprint Retrospective and changes it as needed. In the full model, each line expands a term from the line above: Team = Agents + Coordination Agents = for each agent: Model + Harness + its role, skills and memory Coordination = Orchestration + Shared state + Protocols + Governance Image Al (short for Aletheia, or "truth" in Ancient Greek) is the Scrum Master of the Relentless Raptors, my agent team. He puts every task on a shared task list and never assigns work. Seven Developers, each a specialist agent, claim tasks themselves: a copywriter, a citations specialist, an image maker, a quality assurance (QA) reviewer, two web builders and a designer. I am the Product Owner. I order the Product Backlog and decide what is released. After every story is Done, a separate AI review reads all of the story's records and traces each error to its cause. I call it the story retrospective; it is not the Sprint Retrospective. The team proposes changes to its own rules and tools, and I approve and make them. Three defects from my team's records that started outside the model 1. Two agents saved over each other's work In late October, the plan for a blog post scheduled two tasks at the same time. The copywriter edited the draft to remove machine-sounding text, and the citations agent added the reference list. Both tasks replace the whole document when they save. The two agents read the draft within seconds of each other. The citations agent saved the references two minutes later. The copywriter saved the edited draft 22 minutes later, built from the copy it read before the references existed, and the reference list was gone. The QA agent found the peer-review gap and restored it. The plan put two whole-document writers side by side, and the save tool never checked whether the document had changed since it was read. The story retrospective recommended a save that rejects a stale copy and a plan check that rejects two writers on one document at once. Neither fix has been built yet. A shared editor that merges changes as people type would have kept both edits; these agents saved whole copies instead. 2. Two agents claimed the same task An agent claims a task the way many Developers sign up for work on their Sprint Backlog: in one place everyone can see, with one name on each task. Each claim creates a lock named after the task, and a second agent that tries the same lock is refused. On 23 October, two agents both took the lock for the same planning task. One filed its lock under the story's name and the other under the planning session's name, so both claims succeeded. Both agents planned the story, and the plan checker refused the result. Two days later the claim rule changed: every lock now goes under the session's name, so two claims on one task meet the same lock and the second is refused. 3. Hand-built handoffs failed…

items.title: The Framework is Not the Point
items.summary: Image I am not sure how many times I have explained to my kids that no, they probably won't use Calculus. And maybe they won't need to know the details of Earth Science. Or how Pride and Prejudice ends. But that's not the point. The point of going to High School is to learn how to learn . How to assimilate and analyze data. To find out what you're capable of and to give you confidence that yes, you can do that thing - whatever "that thing" is for you. Scrum has something in common with Calculus, it turns out. Scrum helps teams learn how to learn. The framework of Scrum isn't the end goal. Just implementing Scrum by itself is helpful, but it's only the beginning. When you implement Scrum, you are implementing a way for the Scrum team to learn how to deliver value better. Here's what I mean. Role clarity empowers the team. The Scrum framework includes three accountabilities : the Product Owner (they decide what the team will work on next), Developers (they deliver the product) and a Scrum Master (they facilitate meetings and improve the adoption of Scrum.) The role clarity that comes from this simple framework is enormous. Whenever I see strife on a team, it often comes from a lack of role clarity. Scrum helps teams get beyond that. When it's clear what your job is, only then you can embrace it and get better at it. Scrum events create a feedback loop. The Scrum framework has just enough structure to help teams plan frequently, work together to deliver something, inspect it, and adapt their plan, and talk about how they can do it better next time. That's what the five events of Scrum are all about. They create a feedback loop that helps the Scrum team learn. The artifacts make it clear what the plan for the product is, and who is doing what. Scrum includes artifacts like the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog that provide transparency on what the plan is for the product as well as the team's plan for delivering the Sprint. When you have visibility as to how work is proceeding in the Sprint Backlog, you can come up with ideas on how to improve your work process. And when you know what is in the Product Backlog and where the Product is going, you can better discuss what might be more valuable. Deliver early and often. When you deliver something, you learn a lot about feasibility and also whether it is what the customer really wanted. You're reducing business and technical risk and getting value sooner. When teams use Scrum, they deliver something usable every Sprint . Frequent delivery shortens the learning loop, so you get feedback faster and learn from it. Empiricism means learning by doing. Scrum isn't about just going through the motions. It's about using transparency as a tool that enables the team to inspect what was delivered and learn from it. The engine behind Scrum is Empiricism , a way to learn from experience and adapt based on what is learned. This doesn't get talked about enough. The superpower behind Scrum is that it is a learning engine when it's used effectively. Every artifact provides transparency, and every event is an opportunity to inspect and adapt. When you do that, you learn how to improve value delivery. A clear Product Goal promotes learning. The Scrum framework includes the establishment of a Product Goal. I worked with a consumer products company a few years back, and our Product Goal was to increase sales. The team met to discuss how to achieve it, and we decided to take two paths: increase traffic with SEO and decrease shopping cart abandonment. After every release, we measured the impact of our changes. Having a clear goal and being empowered to meet it meant we ran experiments to see what worked and what didn't. When you work towards a Product Goal, you learn over time what changes are a good step towards that goal, and which are not. And all of that adds up to a lot of learning and continuous improvement - but only when you realize that the framework was never the goal, but merely a means to an end. And that end is delivering value. Conclusion So no, most people will never use Calculus. But that was never the point. The point is learning how to learn. The Scrum framework is no different. When teams use Scrum, they learn how to work together effectively, how to deliver something of value, and they learn how to learn through experimentation and a focus on value delivery.

items.title: When AI Speeds Up Implementation, Test Your Ideas with Small Experiments
items.summary: When AI makes implementation faster, it can be tempting to start the next feature too. But we need to make sure we are not adding unnecessary features. Before asking how to reduce the wait for review and validation, we need to look at how long it takes to get feedback from customers and users. Shorten lead time so that you can get feedback on what you have built sooner. To do that, reduce batch size: the amount of work you take on as a single unit. At the same time, keep work in progress (WIP), work that has been started but not finished, from growing too large. If faster implementation leads us to let WIP grow too large or bundle work into large batches, we risk losing sight of the outcomes customers and users want. Alongside what we can build and how much, we need to examine what customers will be able to achieve. Break Down Work Based on the Customer's Current State Start by understanding what customers and users can achieve today and what they want to achieve. Form a hypothesis grounded in facts about how to move closer to those desired outcomes. Then decide on a unit of work that can yield meaningful feedback. DORA's guidance on working in small batches also explains that small batches let us test hypotheses quickly and revisit assumptions or change direction when needed. It also warns that breaking work into small batches and then regrouping them before testing or release delays feedback. DORA's guidance on working in small batches Breaking work into smaller pieces does not, on its own, mean we will learn from customers. We need to divide it in a way that lets us find out whether we have moved closer to what customers want to achieve. The Information-technology Promotion Agency, Japan (IPA), makes a similar point in its Japanese publication あなたが創る、豊かな未来－Software-Defined Societyの実現に向かって (a guide to realizing a software-defined society). It describes having people actually use a small implementation, then using the results to inform the next hypothesis or improvement. Read the IPA guide (Japanese, PDF p.15) Image Figure 1. Two decisions for faster learning: batch size and WIP. Ground Hypotheses in Facts I believe a hypothesis needs a factual basis. I regard anything based on predictions, speculation, or hunches as guesswork, not a hypothesis. Grounding a hypothesis in facts is what allows us to inspect it through scientific thinking and adapt to what we learn. Do not assume that everything will create value. Nor can we assume that everything will go according to plan. When uncertainty is high and circumstances change, excessive confidence in value or excessive planning can be fatal. AI may implement exactly what we ask for. Even so, if the starting point is off, the results will go in the wrong direction too. Before asking for an implementation, we need to examine which facts informed our thinking and what we concluded from them. Ask for the Evidence Behind Requests to Build Everything at Once When you try to test something on a small scale, managers or stakeholders may ask you to build everything together or follow the original plan. Ask whether they can provide a factual basis for believing that the work can be done as one batch or that the original plan should be followed. In my view, such requests often arise because people lack supporting evidence or do not understand the current facts. Sometimes they are busy and want to make the decision once and be done with it. They are also often held back by past successes and established habits. Checking whether there is supporting evidence takes effort. Still, it cannot be avoided. If it is difficult to raise the question directly, you can ask AI to analyze the situation and use that analysis as a reference. Treat it as input to your examination of the evidence. Run Small Experiments Toward a Near-Term Goal To check results on a small scale without increasing WIP, treat each undertaking as an experiment, not as a task. If you use Agile Kata, begin by understanding the current state. Then set a near-term goal that can be achieved in about one to two weeks, and run small experiments toward it. Agile Kata One to two weeks is a rough guide for reaching the near-term goal, not a timebox. It does not prescribe the duration of an individual experiment. Test a smaller step toward the goal, then reassess the current state each time. Image Figure 2. Small experiments turn facts into learning toward a near-term goal. Understand the current state after each experiment, then run the next experiment toward the goal. Repeating this helps us obtain customer feedback while keeping WIP appropriately constrained. Calling something an experiment does not itself constrain WIP. Decisions about starting the next piece of work also need to be made within this learning process. The Kanban Guide calls for explicitly controlling WIP from start to finish and starting new work when there is a clear signal that capacity is available to take it on. items.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
items.summary: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. items.title: AI Adoption Failures: Why Your Successful AI Pilot Is No Reason to Scale
items.summary: TL;DR: A Successful AI Pilot Proves Nothing Thesis : This article explains seven AI adoption failures that follow a successful AI pilot, from unready data to overloaded reviewers and premature cuts, and how practitioners set the standard, collect the evidence, and inspect the results before scaling anything. Your AI pilot worked: the demo impressed the steering committee, the time savings on the slide looked fantastic, and the sponsor is already drafting the rollout budget. However, the AI pilot answered a narrower question than the budget. It showed that the technology can do the task under test conditions, with clean data, a hand-picked team, and a process that mainly exists in the standard operating procedures. Two questions remain open, and nobody has collected evidence for them: whether ordinary teams can run the workflow reliably, and whether expanding beyond the pilot pays off. Here are seven AI adoption failures that keep recurring in legacy organizations in 2026, each with a warning sign you can check this week, a countermeasure, plus five questions for the scaling decision itself. You do not need to own the budget to use them, because the evidence a scaling decision needs comes from the people closest to the work: they agree on the quality standard, for example, using the AI Definition of Done before the trial, collect the evidence while the workflow runs, and inspect the delegation over time in an AI Delegation Audit. Spoiler alert for the seasoned agile practitioner: If you lived through an Agile transformation, most of the failures will look familiar. History rhymes, and AI, as Agile, is no exception. Image Disclaimer : I read Charniak/McDermott’s book on "Artificial Intelligence" decades ago; of course, I use AI for research, translations, proofreading, challenging story arcs and article structures, creating artifacts such as graphics, and summarization. It is a production tool, not a substitute for thinking. 🗞 Shall I notify you about articles like this one? Awesome! You can sign up here for the ‘Food for Agile Thought’ newsletter and join 35,000-plus subscribers . The AI Pilot Succeeded, and That Is the Problem A small, well-designed AI experiment that fails is cheap: it costs a few weeks, a small budget, and some pride, and it usually teaches the organization something about its data and its processes. A successful pilot, however, can become expensive because it gives the sponsor what looks like evidence for a rollout the pilot never tested. Then, once the rollout begins, the AI meets the organization as it actually runs, and the expected outcome turns into escalations, workarounds, and change requests that nobody put on the original slide. None of this makes the AI pilot worthless. Testing a narrow technical hypothesis under controlled conditions is legitimate, and curated data and motivated volunteers may be exactly the right setup. The failure happens one step later, when the organization uses the result to answer a question the pilot never asked. There are three questions hidden behind "the AI pilot worked," and each of them needs different evidence: Can the technology do this task? Evidence: performance under specified test conditions, which is what a pilot usually delivers. Can ordinary teams run this workflow reliably? Evidence: results on representative cases, the exceptions, the support requests, and the time people spend preparing the input and reviewing the output. Should we scale the AI pilot? Evidence: value that holds over months, quality the recipients accept, the full operating cost including review, and an accountable owner who can stop the workflow when it fails. Too many rollout budgets get approved on the answer to the first question alone, resulting in preventable AI Adoption failures. To keep this concrete, I will follow one hypothetical AI pilot through the article (the organization and its numbers are invented): an AI drafts the weekly stakeholder status report from Jira for one product team, the team's product manager reviews each draft, the report goes out in 20 minutes instead of 3 hours, and the sponsor now wants the same for all 40 product teams by next quarter. In an earlier article on why AI transformations rhyme with Agile transformations , I described the greenfield showcase as one of five patterns the two share. The seven failures below follow once the applause fades, grouped by when they occur. Your Part When You Do Not Own the Budget If you are a Scrum Master, Project Manager, Product Owner, Product Manager, or Agile Coach, you probably do not decide about reskilling budgets or the rollout plan. Nevertheless, you sit closer to the evidence than anyone on the steering committee, and you can do five things for one expansion decision: Observe how the workflow actually runs, workarounds included. items.title: AI - More Feedback, Less Direction
items.summary: Image In a refinement I ran this year, the team asked to extend the session because there was too much to discuss. Every CI pipeline flag, every behavioral analytics alert, every AI-synthesized user interview summary had produced something worth examining. The Product Owner and the analysts had all prepared detailed, AI-generated views, and each one looked at a different aspect and presented it as the most important. Mostly they were disjointed data points. We ran over time and still ended without a decision, because the team had spent the Sprint drowning in feedback and arrived with less clarity than they started with. That was a refinement, but the Sprint Review has the same problem, and I now see it in a growing number of teams. Two Layers, One System Scrum was designed around a problem that has not changed: how do you make good decisions before you have enough information to be certain? It answers with two mechanisms working together. The first layer is social, getting the right people talking at the right time, in the right amount. The Product Owner holds direction and is accountable for what gets built. Developers own quality and push back on what cannot be built safely. The Scrum Master keeps the team learning so it does not turn into a feature factory. The events are the scheduled moments where feedback becomes shared understanding. The second is technical, and it works through two checkpoints from the Scrum Guide Expansion Pack [4]. The Definition of Output Done settles quality before anything moves on. The Definition of Outcome Done sits one level up. It asks whether what shipped moved the metric it was meant to move, and what the release revealed that nobody predicted. Both layers exist to turn raw signal into decisions a team can act on. What AI Compresses AI is compressing both layers at once, though the effects differ on each side. On the technical side, AI code review and automated testing turn hours of waiting into minutes. The 2025 DORA report found a positive relationship between AI adoption and delivery throughput [1]. AI adoption still has a negative relationship with delivery stability. DORA traces that to teams lacking "strong automated testing, mature version control practices, and fast feedback loops," where extra change volume "leads to instability." DORA never mentions Scrum, so the mapping is mine. Still, that list reads almost like a description of Scrum's technical layer. On the product side, analytics, AI-summarized user research and live dashboards let stakeholders watch the product all the time, and they form opinions at any hour. A team that reads that data as proof of delivery is still doing project work. Feedback Fatigue In the teams I work with, I keep seeing what I would call feedback fatigue. The individual signals are mostly accurate, yet their volume has outrun the team's ability to make sense of them. By the Sprint Review the team has so much raw signal it no longer knows what question to bring to stakeholders. The cause is simple arithmetic. Every signal has to be read, judged, and then acted on or set aside, and that sorting costs attention whether the signal matters or not. AI has made signals cheap, so the sorting grows with every new tool. The number of real decisions a team can make in a Sprint has not grown at all. Most signals also arrive without the question they answer, so someone must first work out what each one is evidence for. Past a certain volume, the hours go into sorting and almost none are left for deciding. The Sprint was built to process feedback into something actionable. A Review condenses a Sprint's worth of signal into one conversation about what changed and what it means for what comes next. When feedback arrived slower than the Sprint, there was rarely enough new information to argue about. Now that it arrives continuously, the Sprint Goal does a different job. It is the filter that decides which signals the team acts on now and which wait. Nothing says finished work has to wait for the Review either. The Scrum Guide [5] lets a team deliver an Increment before the Sprint ends and says the Review "should never be considered a gate to releasing value." A team that releases as it goes can arrive with data collected from real use, and the Review becomes a conversation about that data instead of a demo. I expect Sprint length to shrink as well. When building and feedback both take hours instead of days, a team will accept less time between inspections, and the Guide already allows shorter Sprints "to generate more learning cycles." The Sprint Goal still stays fixed inside the Sprint, because a goal that moves with every signal gives the team no direction. Scope can shift beneath it, and if the goal itself turns obsolete, the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint, which costs little on a short one. items.title: Are You Overstepping?
items.summary: Image For a Scrum Team, role clarity can make the difference between a low performing and a high performing team. In fact, whenever I see strife on a team, it almost always stems from a lack of role clarity. When people step on each other's toes - even with the best of intentions - it can create tension on a team. In this article, we will provide common oversteps for the Product Owner, Developers and Scrum Masters and what you can do to fix them. Product Owner Oversteps The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product by focusing on what to deliver, not how to deliver it. Solutioning. If your Product Backlog describes not only what you want, but how to deliver it, you may be overstepping. If you're putting table names in your Product Backlog items, you may be getting too far into the weeds. Instead, focus on what you want and why it matters. Let the Developers figure out how best to deliver it. Preloading the Sprint. If the Product Owner is building out a detailed Sprint Backlog before Sprint Planning event starts, they may be taking away from the creativity and problem-solving aspects that belong to Developers. Instead, come to Sprint Planning prepared to discuss what's most valuable and why. Give the Developers room to figure out what's possible. Roadmap is not flexible. It's one thing to have a roadmap. It's another to demand that the Scrum Team deliver it, come hell or high water. A roadmap is a guess. I'm not saying we can't have deadlines, but I am saying that how we get there should change as we learn more. You may need to remove scope or add budget to meet your Product Goal. Why are these oversteps? The Product Owner should be minding the store, not stocking the shelves. They should be looking two, three, or more Sprints ahead, thinking about where the product needs to go, rather than getting caught up in tactical details that the Developers can handle. Developer Oversteps Developers are accountable for creating a usable Increment every Sprint and determining how to turn Product Backlog items into value. Unilaterally deciding to work on technical debt. I've seen Developers decide to spend an entire Sprint cleaning up code because they believe it's important. And they may be right! But when Developers make significant decisions about how to spend the team's time without involving the Product Owner, they're taking away from the Product Owner's ability to maximize value. Working on lower priority work because it's in the same module. I've seen Developers pull lower-priority work into the Sprint (mid-Sprint!) simply because they were already working in that module. I appreciate efficiency, but working on lower priority work is never going to be efficient. Just one more fix. Don't pull work into the Sprint unless you believe that it can be developed and tested by the end of the Sprint. And if you are pulling work into the Sprint mid-Sprint, talk to your teammates before you make that decision. Why are these oversteps? Developers want to improve the quality of the product, work efficiently, and get as much done as possible. Those are all good things! But when Developers make these decisions on their own, they can undermine the Product Owner's accountability for maximizing value and the team's ability to meet the Sprint Goal. Scrum Master Oversteps The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum and improving the Scrum Team's effectiveness. I know from experience that it can be easy to get overzealous when you're trying to help. Becoming the Team's Administrator. I once tried to help a Scrum team by submitting all their security requests for them. Pretty soon I got behind and I became a bottleneck. Don't try to do everyone's work for them. You aren't doing anyone any favors and in fact you are creating a sense of disempowerment. Assigning work to Developers. When the Scrum Master starts assigning tasks or deciding how work should be distributed, they're stepping into the Developers' accountability. How can Developers learn to self-manage if someone else is always telling them what to do? Running every Event. It's true that the Scrum Guide says that the Scrum Master should facilitate events when requested or needed. But it doesn't mean you own every event. Start with letting the Developers run the Daily Scrum. Take turns leading the Retrospective. You may be surprised at how much more powerful these events become when you realize that the Scrum team is full of creative leaders. Your goal should be to help the Scrum Team become less dependent on you, not more. Conclusion Most oversteps happen with the best of intentions. We want to help! But sometimes the best way to help is to step back and give someone else the opportunity to do their job. So, the next time you find yourself stepping into someone else's accountability, ask yourself: Am I really helping, or am I getting in the way?

items.title: What Should Managers Evaluate If They Want People to Rethink Their Work with AI?
items.summary: Microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index surveyed 20,000 knowledge workers across 10 countries who use AI at work. In the survey, 45% said it felt safer to focus on current goals than to redesign their work with AI. 13% said they were rewarded for redesigning work with AI even when it did not produce the expected results. Survey findings and methodology These figures are not limited to a specific country. They do, however, raise a question about how we approach everyday goals and evaluation when asking people to change the way they work with AI. Keep Business Success at the Center Business goals matter. It is natural to consider AI as a means of achieving them, but the means must not become the end. Business success needs to remain at the center. We should begin by developing a strategy for achieving it. If existing business goals or strategy are unclear, that is likely to indicate a weak strategy. This is where facts matter. We need to start by understanding the current state based on information and data. We must not discount the current state simply because we have made a plan and believe we should follow it, or because we have invested so much in the plan that we feel we cannot turn back. Being in the Execution Phase can itself lead us to discount the current state. We need to pause and step back from execution to reassess what is happening and distinguish facts from opinions, assumptions, and emotions. Customer Outcomes and Organizational Capability Understanding the outcomes users and customers want is essential to business success. Customers can do something they could not do before. Something that once took time and effort becomes easy to accomplish. These changes show up in customer satisfaction and engagement. To understand the current state, we need to examine the facts with these desired outcomes in mind. At the same time, looking only at current value is not enough. Does the organization have the capability to achieve those outcomes and improve them further? We need to examine that as well. We also need AI’s help to collect and analyze this information. Frequent learning is essential to achieving desired outcomes. The reason to explore product development with generative AI is also to learn quickly so that we can improve value. We should use AI to improve value and to learn faster, not because it is popular. Evaluate the Team’s Self-Directed Initiative The first change managers need to make is to become able to base decisions on data. This will likely require a shift from a plan-driven approach to a goal-driven one that anticipates change. Managers set out the strategy and strategic goals: the direction to pursue. The team then takes the initiative to understand its current state, set its own immediate goals, and work toward them. This self-directed initiative is what managers should evaluate. Because results do not appear right away, what managers ask of the team should be limited to this initiative. At the organizational level, however, evaluation should focus on the customer outcomes discussed earlier. Table 1. Team evaluation, organizational evaluation, and managers’ responsibility Customer outcomes fluctuate, so we have to keep measuring the indicators and examine trends. If managers believe the team’s own goals are not connected to the strategic goals, they can provide support. Managers Should Reconsider Their Own Goals Too Measurement and the team’s work may reveal a need to change the goals managers have set. When that happens, managers themselves should reconsider those goals. Evaluating the team is only part of a manager’s role. Managers need to take responsibility for making decisions at a more strategic level and revisiting goals. The team understands its current state, sets immediate goals, and works toward them. Managers use information from that work and from customer outcomes to reconsider strategic decisions. Understanding the current state, setting goals, and using the facts learned to reconsider goals and ways of working are fundamental to Evidence-Based Management (EBM). EBM Guide Figure 1. Revisiting goals based on facts If you want people to change their work with AI, you need to examine both what managers evaluate and what they themselves are responsible for reconsidering. Support the team’s self-directed initiative, keep examining customer outcomes, and make decisions based on data. What matters is using AI within that process. Questions to Ask About Your Own Approach As you reconsider your approach, ask these questions: Are we distinguishing facts from opinions and assumptions about the outcomes customers currently experience? When evaluating the team, are we looking at its initiative in understanding the current state and setting its own immediate goals? Are the immediate goals the team sets for itself connected to the strategic goals? Are managers themselves revisiting goals based on measurement and the team’s work? Zu diesem besonderen Anlass gratuliere Bürgermeister Alois Zetsch herzlich und überbrachte die Glückwünsche der Gemeinde. Wir wünschen dem Jubelpaar weiterhin alles Gute, Gesundheit und viele schöne gemeinsame Jahre. Das könnte ebenfalls interessant sein: Alles Gute zum 85. Geburtstag, Roland Moser

items.summary: Seit zehn Jahren lebt Anja Böck in Berlin. Doch auch nach zahlreichen Stationen im Ausland ist Niederösterreich für sie Heimat geblieben. Im Interview erzählt sie von nostalgischen Erinnerungen an Korneuburg und Stockerau, typisch niederösterreichischen Kindheitserlebnissen und davon, wie sie ihre Heimat erst mit etwas Abstand richtig schätzen gelernt hat. items.title: SpaceX will beide Raketenteile auffangen
items.summary: Der Rakete Starship des Raumfahrtunternehmens SpaceX von Elon Musk steht ein wichtiger Testflug bevor: In der Nacht auf Samstag (MEZ) sollen erstmals beide Raketenteile von Greifarmen wieder aufgefangen werden – ein entscheidender Versuch, ein vollständig wiederverwendbares Raketensystem zu schaffen.

items.title: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago
items.summary: A mysterious force driving the expansion of the Universe may have undergone a dramatic reversal billions of years ago. Scientists exploring an overlooked branch of an alternative gravity theory discovered that dark energy could have switched from negative to positive roughly 9.5 billion years ago, potentially changing how we understand cosmic history.

items.title: Weinsegnung im Familienweingut Karl Spielauer
items.summary: Am 10.11.2026 lud das Familienweingut Karl Spielauer zur traditionellen Weinsegnung ins Heurigenlokal. Pfarrer Marius Zediu segnete den neuen Jahrgang. Karl Spielauer berichtete über das herausfordernde Weingartenjahr. Im Anschluss wurde auf den „jungen Wein“, die gute Zusammenarbeit mit den Lesehelfern und dem Heurigenpersonal sowie auf die erfolgreiche Renovierung angestoßen. Das könnte ebenfalls interessant sein: Hinweise aus der Bevölkerung sind willkommen

items.title: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse
items.summary: The massive solar storm that illuminated skies worldwide in May 2024 has uncovered an unexpected twist: Earth's own atmosphere may have helped make the storm so powerful. Satellite measurements revealed that roughly 85% of the charged particles fueling the disturbance originated from Earth's upper atmosphere rather than the solar wind. Scientists also detected an extraordinary 40% weakening of Earth's magnetic field high above the planet.

items.title: Zahl der Tierversuche in Österreich leicht gesunken
items.summary: Die Zahl der in Österreich in Versuchen verwendeten Tiere ist im vergangenen Jahr erneut leicht zurückgegangen: 2025 wurden 188.367 Tiere für diesen Zweck eingesetzt, das waren um 3,83 Prozent weniger als im Jahr zuvor (195.876).

items.title: Stakeholder Management: The Core of the Product Owner Role
items.summary: In almost every training session, there is a product owner who has been putting off the conversation with their toughest stakeholder for three sprints already. Odds are you have one just like that. You know exactly which conversation it is and what is at stake. You just aren't having it. That’s not a failure on your part as a PO. You are doing your job just fine, but your week is consumed by stakeholders who are all screaming that their request is priority 1. Stakeholder management is still too often dismissed as a "soft skill": an afterthought squeezed somewhere between refining your product backlog and running a tight sprint planning. What Research Says About Stakeholder Management In our National Product Owner Survey ( Nationaal Product Owner Onderzoek ), Dutch product owners have consistently cited stakeholder management as both the most critical and the most challenging aspect of their profession for years. It also tops the list of what POs want to learn themselves even ahead of product vision and roadmapping. Image Beneath that lies a metric that is less frequently linked to stakeholders: one-third of a product owner's workload consists of unplanned, ad hoc work. That is more than a day and a half each week that nobody accounted for. You feel it on Friday afternoon when the user story you planned to pick up on Monday is still untouched. In my experience, a significant portion of that starts with a stakeholder who got to your desk before you reached out to theirs. Two Different Lenses Why is that conversation often so difficult? Because as a product owner, you look at the world through a product lens : you think in terms of vision, value, team performance, backlog order, and technical feasibility. But your stakeholder is looking through an entirely different lens. They look through the lens of their domain, their targets, and the pressure coming down from above. Image You look at the world through a product lens! If you expect a stakeholder to put on your product lens, you are going to "lose" the conversation. You’ll be talking past each other! Jokingly, I often say in training: Stakeholders sometimes act just like kids right before the holidays : they all believe they’ve been the best-behaved and deserve the most presents. Taking into account the total budget or the team’s capacity? That’s your job, not theirs. And if you don't push back, you simply become part of someone else's plan. True stakeholder management is not about waving your roadmap around and saying "no." Of course, those are important elements where a roadmap helps you push back. But you are a product owner, not a product dictator. It’s about building a partnership . And that only happens when you address both sides of their needs: The business need (what information, KPIs, or outcomes do they need for their role?). The personal need (what drives them as a human being in this conversation?). Not a Single "Type," but Shifting Needs It is crucial to realize that you cannot put people into a box as a single "type" of stakeholder. It is about needs , and one person can have multiple needs simultaneously or sequentially, depending on the situation or topic: Sometimes there is a need for "Power" / Status: They want to know: what's in it for me? They test you in the first few minutes. Show immediately how your product helps them achieve their goals. Sometimes there is a need for Certainty: They want to minimize risks. Take the pressure off by walking them through your iterative approach and leveraging their domain knowledge. Sometimes there is a need for "Social" / Relationship: They want to connect first. Accept that the first 20 minutes will be about the weekend; only then do you earn their goodwill. Sometimes there is a need for Order or Realization: They want structure, action, tight agendas, and zero surprises. And there is always the "undervalued" need: Genuine recognition. Every human being wants to be seen and appreciated for their contribution and responsibility. Most POs find this very challenging. How to Actually Have That Postponed Conversation (and Boost Your Effectiveness) Put yourself in your stakeholder's shoes (and lenses) What is truly important to them? What pressure are they feeling from their own constituents? Consider using an Empathy Map (see image below) to separate hard observations from your own assumptions and interpretations. Anticipate upfront which need is central What personal and business needs does this specific stakeholder have right now? Address that directly in your preparation and communication style. Determine the exact conversation you need to have It is rarely about the prioritization order between two user stories. What it’s really about is: what information do they want to receive, through which channel, at what frequency, and in what format to satisfy their needs? items.title: Der Weltuntergang ist abgesagt
items.summary: Am 13. November 2026 geht die Welt unter. So lautete zumindest eine Prognose aus dem Jahr 1960. Der aus Österreich stammende Systemtheoretiker Heinz von Foerster formulierte diese düstere Voraussage – nicht ganz ernst gemeint allerdings. Eine Konferenz in Wien greift seine Gedanken auf und spinnt sie weiter, mit Blick in die Zukunft.

items.title: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that where men get their protein may be linked to their testosterone levels. Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.

items.title: Herkunft von Hantavirus weiter unklar
items.summary: Ein tödlicher Hantavirus-Ausbruch auf einem Kreuzfahrtschiff im Südatlantik sorgte im Frühling 2026 für weltweite Beunruhigung. Nun liefert eine im Fachjournal „Science“ veröffentlichte Studie neue Erkenntnisse dazu. Wo sich die Passagiere ursprünglich ansteckten, bleibt allerdings unklar.

items.title: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
items.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.

items.title: Grundstein für 3-D-Karte des Kosmos
items.summary: Die Europäische Weltraumorganisation (ESA) hat am Donnerstag umfassende Beobachtungsdaten des Weltraumteleskops Euclid veröffentlicht. Sie bilden den Grundstein für die größte 3-D-Karte des Kosmos.

items.title: Elefanten: Ernährung beeinflusst Mikrobiom
items.summary: Im Elefantendarm dominieren Bakterien, die Spezialisten für den Abbau von Pflanzenmaterial sind. Wie eine Ernährungsumstellung bei Elefanten das Darmmikrobiom verändern kann, zeigt nun eine Pilotstudie an Elefanten aus dem Tiergarten Schönbrunn in Wien.

items.title: Adipositas-Diagnose braucht mehr als BMI
items.summary: Wie schwer und wie groß man ist, sagt wenig über die Gesundheit eines Menschen aus. In diesem Sinn sollte auch die Diagnose Adipositas nicht allein anhand des Body-Mass-Index (BMI) definiert werden, fordern Fachleute. Eine neue Studie untermauert diese Kritik am BMI und zeigt, welche Vorteile eine genauere Diagnose bringen würde.

items.title: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
items.summary: Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from space.

items.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.

items.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
items.summary: A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not.

items.title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields
items.summary: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has revealed a surprising secret hidden within the chaos of space: turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales. The discovery exposes an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.

items.title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
items.summary: A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation.

items.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
items.summary: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.

items.title: A radical theory says the universe is twice as old as we thought
items.summary: A provocative new cosmological model suggests the Universe could be 26.7 billion years old and might not need dark matter or dark energy to explain its behavior. University of Ottawa researchers tested the theory against several major astronomical observations, finding that it could explain galaxy rotation, cosmic expansion, and the formation of early elements.

items.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke
items.summary: New research involving more than 440,000 Americans links cannabis use to increased cardiovascular risk, with occasional users showing 40% higher odds of reporting a history of stroke. The findings suggest that even infrequent marijuana use may warrant concern, although researchers have not established that cannabis directly causes strokes or heart disease.

items.title: Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images
items.summary: A breakthrough in telescope imaging could reveal countless alien worlds that have been hiding in plain sight. Scientists developed a new technique that uses a digital twin of the James Webb Space Telescope to remove the overwhelming glare of stars, making faint exoplanets two to 15 times easier to detect than with conventional methods. The technology has already uncovered a previously hidden planet in existing telescope data and could reveal many more.
